title: JP Morgan, Fidelity, and Schwab (and the like) are set to rake in billion of dollars in fees, charging people to use their own data; that might sound bad, but experts say the banks mostly wear white hats on this issue - RIABiz
content: With pro-enterprise arguments on both sides, the wrangling was strung out for six years, but incoming CFPB Director Brian Johnson will settle on a 'structured fudge' that enrages some fintechs but also brings quality data into the market on a systematized basis. Wall Street and Main Street firms like Schwab, Fidelity and JP Morgan are set to prevail in a war for the right to charge investors perhaps billions of dollars to use their own data to understand their financial transactions. It's difficult to swallow because data that was mostly always free is now marked up to retail. It's your data. Yet, looks can be deceiving. Big, Financial's plan to collect data is not only fair as presented, but a likely ‘no-brainer’ advance for the industry – paying a little more to get much better data through a sustainable, stable process. At issue is the Consumer Financial Protection Board's (CFPB) Rule 1033, known as the Personal Financial Data Rights rule. It's a banking regulation designed to give consumers free electronic access to their financial data and the power to share it securely with apps and other financial tools. The rule, however, is currently stalled and undergoing a full reevaluation after a federal court enjoined its enforcement, and new agency leadership moved to reconsider its terms. But banks will soon net the “enshrined” right to levy data fees on financial technology companies, if the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) rules in their favor next month, as expected. See: JP Morgan hustles Plaid for a deal. The companies have been campaigning since the CFPB began mulling fee restrictions in Nov. 2020. By 2024, their efforts looked in vain, after the CFPB moved to ban them from charging data-hungry fintechs and aggregators. Then the Trump administration threw out the baby and the bathwater. It paused the Biden-era rule, giving the giants a second chance. They quickly took advantage, using the pause to strong-arm aggregators into paying data fees, and establish the fees as a fait accompli. CFPB Director Brian Johnson is set to support permanent data fees – a volte face that the CFPB is expected to confirm soon, multiple reports indicate. Expect the final rule to be a “structured fudge” says Will Trout, director of securities and investments and Datos Insights, in an email. It's likely to “enshrine” the right for banks to charge fees, which is “a win for the banks.” The ruling will likely include “some form of reasonableness, or cost-basis standard attached, as a partial concession to fintech and consumer interests," Trout continues. "Whether that standard has teeth is doubtful given who is running the agency,” he adds. Yet what makes it reasonable is that the freeloaders are forced to pay, and the free-for-all of credential-sharing and screen-scraping robots is curtailed, according to JP Morgan. “The charging is specifically for data aggregators, not customers, and is designed to incentivize more responsible data access behaviors,” the JP Morgan spokesperson says in an email exchange. “Data middlemen were profiting from customer data without contributing to the infrastructure that supports it, so our fee agreements ensure that those who benefit from the data – the aggregators – also contribute to its security,” the spokesperson explains. The wrangling over data fees goes to the heart of wealth management – given the industry's dependence on aggregated client data. Tired of having their screens scraped, Schwab and Fidelity launch API initiatives  to curtail the practice -- rewarding some, but not all scrapers with cleaner data Despite their initial support for Trump's early 2025 dismantling of the Biden-era regulation, Donald Trump Jr. and other MAGA cohorts – including George Mason University Foundation law professor, Todd Zywick, and Tyler Winklevoss, the outspoken founder and CEO of cryptocurrency exchange Gemini – also find themselves on the same side as the pre-Trump Consumer Federation of America, and Democratic and free data activists. But the fee naysayers are missing the forest for the trees, says Terry Hong, CEO and co-founder of SSG Engineering, who, full disclosure, does engineering work for RIABiz. “You pay, but you get clean data and your engineering time back. API and partnership deals existed in pockets, but this makes them the standard. The hidden cost of scraping was always the army of engineers at Plaid or Yodlee maintaining it. Trading that for a fee and reinvesting the time in higher-value products is a no-brainer to me,” he says. “If I were Plaid, I'd be pleased that I can just pay and get clean data but I'd be very unhappy if it whittles away at my moat, which is my ability to throw engineers at the problem. Meat-grinder-engineering.” Investors have bid down Plaid's value in the private markets, with its recent funding done at $8 billion after raising capital at a $13.4 billion valuation in 2021, according to a July 1 article in Bloomberg. See: Finance App Network Maker Plaid Is Said to Consider US IPO The use of bank infrastructure by Plaid and others is more pernicious than garden-variety freeloading, a JPMorgan systems employee wrote last week in an internal memo to retail payments head Melissa Feldsher, according to CNBC. “Aggregators are accessing customer data multiple times daily, even when the customer is not actively using the app,” the staffer said. “These access requests are massively taxing our systems.” So tangled had the issue become that though the fee approvals by CFPB end a Biden-era CFPB push to keep data free, and the final line of resistance against the change came from ‘crypto’ advocates like Tyler Winklevoss, and Trump Jr. What lit crypto advocates' hair on fire is that for crypto to have value, it must be interoperable with the banking system, and the CFPB's reported plan to allow "transaction" volume fees jacks up the cost of interoperability, according to a June 19 article in the Washington Reporter. “For crypto platforms, specifically, which rely on seamless account linking to enable on-ramping, even modest per-call fees can impose costs that are prohibitive relative to low-dollar transaction sizes – effectively pricing less wealthy Americans out of digital asset participation,” Alex Rampell, general partner at Andreessen Horowitz, wrote in a July 31, 2025 blog post. “If it suddenly costs $10 to move $100 into a Coinbase or Robinhood account, fewer people will do it; or if it costs $10 to get a cheaper loan from a fintech, consumers may be forced to take a worse one from [an] incumbent bank, instead," he explains. “Banksters are trying to kill fintech and crypto companies," added Winklevoss in a Jul. 20 X post. “They want to take away your right to access your banking data for free via-third party apps like Plaid, and instead charge you, and fintechs, exorbitant fees to access your data. This is the kind of egregious regulatory capture that kills innovation, hurts the American consumer, and is bad for America,” he adds. JP Morgan hustles Plaid for a deal in bitter fight over 'free data,' with Wells and PNC encouraged, while Fidelity, Schwab also force fintechs to pay up or pound sand as part of 'deeper battle' Fidelity just dropped the hammer on screen scrapers to cheers, but some firms, like Plaid, are holdouts and the CFPB may wield the final gavel Tired of having their screens scraped, Schwab and Fidelity launch API initiatives  to curtail the practice -- rewarding some, but not all scrapers with cleaner data Indeed, Mint went the way of the dodo bird as free access went away. See: Embattled Mint.com is shutting for good, weeks after Fidelity finally cut off free, screen-scraped data that was at the heart of its business model Pontera experienced a serious setback when Fidelity largely cut it off from its 401(k) recordkeeping data. See: Pontera's last-bid gambit to turn Fidelity credential-sharing ban into an 'investor rights issue,' falls flat, and now Schwab and others are turning a deaf ear as bans spread A number of trade associations, including the Financial Technology Association, the Blockchain Association, the National Retail Federation have also stated that the new CFPB Rule 1033 is likely an “attack” on consumer rights and freedoms. Yet, Fidelity, which is itself a crypto pioneer, openly supports the Trump CFPB efforts. See: After five-year stealth project, Fidelity goes big-time into crypto-asset custody with standalone company. Fidelity just dropped the hammer on screen scrapers to cheers, but some firms, like Plaid, are holdouts and the CFPB may wield the final gavel “The crypto and fintech crowd … [are] casualties of a broader CFPB demolition they applauded for other reasons, [then they] got caught in the blast radius." "The banks' fraud and infrastructure argument isn't confected – a zero-cost access regime socializes real costs onto them. Where it becomes suspect is when fees are set at competition-deterrence levels rather than cost-recovery levels,” he explains. “The fintech and crypto side is right that uncapped fees are an innovation tax, but they're weak messengers given their prior posture.” The Trump administration also deserves praise for refusing to use regulation to shield its supporters, because the Biden-era Rule 1033 forced Wall Street to bear both the risks of managing and distributing data, and all of the cost, says Ari Sonneberg, partner at Boston, Mass. law firm, Wagner Law Group. "I get why fintechs are upset, but the argument that banks should absorb billions of dollars in infrastructure and fraud costs to subsidize their competitors isn’t really a consumer protection argument," Sonneberg explains in an email exchange. “The administration understands that there is a real market problem that needs to be addressed by regulation … [and its] expected approach – allowing cost-recovery fees with guardrails – actually seems quite reasonable. It’s not a blank check for JPMorgan to charge whatever it wants,” he adds. The new CFPB rule 1033, once established, is also likely to prove one of Johnson's signature policies. The incoming director is working to finalize a series of initiatives developed by his predecessor, Acting Director Russell Vought, who is expected to stay on as an advisor. Vought, a co-author of President Trump’s ‘Project 2025’ manifesto, has also pressed ahead with the new version of rule 1033, despite the fact that many of its loudest critics are vocal supporters of his broader deregulatory agenda – an agenda that includes regulatory cuts, and a fraught and ongoing battle to fire up to 90% of the CFPB’s workforce. Yet, RIAs could suffer expense dislocations, analysts say. The modern RIA is far more than – and sometimes not even – a portfolio manager, and its service model depends on several data-hungry tools, including financial planning software, like eMoney, RightCapital and MoneyGuidePro, account aggregators like Plaid, Yodlee, or ByAllAccounts, and portfolio reporting tools like Orion, Black Diamond and Tamarac. The new data fees will exert upward pressure on fees, and mergers with larger competitors, reducing competition on both price and service levels, Trout explains. "For RIAs specifically, account aggregation and reporting tools will face margin pressure … through a slow, multi-year transmission. Planning and tax software is more exposed; newer entrants … [have] less negotiating scale … [but] the biggest structural risk is consolidation among aggregators. “Higher data costs favor Plaid and Finicity-Mastercard, and disadvantage smaller competitors … [which] means less innovation, and less optionality in the RIA technology stack over time. [It will be a] slow squeeze, not a sudden shock, but real,” Trout concludes. The impact on RIAs, investors, and retail and corporate banking clients also hinges on how the CFPB decides to regulate ‘reasonable’ fees, and whether financial technology firms decide to pass on increased costs to their clients, analysts say. Managing data comes with “huge value,” as well as costs, so it “comes down to how greedy all of the parties get," says Andrew Besheer, founder and principal of Bronxville, N.Y. consultancy Besheer & Associates. "It could, absolutely" harm the RIA software industry, or, indeed, the fledgling finance-focused ‘AI’ industry, “but it hasn’t yet, even with the big banks fees already in place," he says, in an email. [Editor’s note: When the CFPB paused implementation of the Biden-era Rule 1033, JP Morgan negotiated fee deals with firms, including Plaid and Yodlee] “That said, there's clearly a risk that the banks decide that this is an opportunity to create an extinction event for a breed of competitor," Besheer adds. Banks, RIA custodians, and representative trade bodies like SIFMA – Schwab and Fidelity are members – have also repeatedly stated they only intend to charge financial technology companies for ‘fair use,’ and that they have no plans to limit consumer access to data. "SIFMA reiterates its support for a consumer’s right to access financial information … [but] data providers should be permitted to charge fees ... to ensure that costs are allocated efficiently and fairly, the trade association states, in an Oct. 21, 2025 letter. “The CFPB should allow data providers to offset out of pocket expenses … [and] to generally recover reasonable costs incurred in providing covered data to authorized third parties,” adds Fidelity executive vice president and general counsel, Jonathan Chiel, in a 2023 letter disputing the Biden-era rule 1033. Yet acquiescing to big banks and RIA custodians carries risk, even if it is “probably not catastrophic, unless fee caps fail to materialize," says Trout. “The pre-aggregation era of siloed systems was bad for banks too, but the deals struck so far were struck when regulatory threat still existed,” he explains. “The risk is not that JPMorgan immediately raises fees to predatory levels. It is that permanent enshrinement of the right to charge, with no meaningful floor, compounds slowly … [as] the discipline that kept fees below competition-deterrence levels weakens. "The people who helped dismantle the guardrails are only now noticing because it is their ox being gored,” he says. RIABiz, Mill Valley, California Copyright © 2009-2026 RIABiz Inc.
